# Solid - Local Axes

Form:  Solid Local Axis, Solid Advanced Axes

Use the Assign menu > Solid > Local Axes command to specify the local axes for the selected solid(s).

1. Select one or more [solid objects](../../Edit/Extrude.md) to be assigned the same local axes.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid > Local Axes command to access the Solid Local Axis form.
3. Type in a value for rotation angles about the Z, Y’ and X” axes, in degrees (Y’ and X” are used as axes names instead of Y and X to emphasize that after an angle about Z has been specified, the local X and Y will change as a result).

Check the Use default check box if the Global definition is to be used for the local axes.

If appropriate, check the Advanced Axes check box and click the Advanced button to access the Solid Advanced Axis form. Use that form to refine the specification of the local axes for the selected object(s).

1. - Local Axes Type options.  When the Default option is selected, the other areas of the form are not available and no further input is required. This is the default. When the Advanced option is selected, the input required on the form changes depending on the options selected in the Axial Reference Vector Specified by and Plane Reference Vector Specified by areas of the form.
   - Local Plane drop-down list. Select the local plane for the solid from the drop-down list.
   - Axial Reference Vector Specified by options.  Choose one of the following options to specify how the axial reference vector will be specified:
   - - Coordinate Direction option.  When this option is selected, the form will display a Coordinate System drop-down list and an Axial Coordinate Direction area and Direction drop-down list.  Select the coordinate system for the reference vector and then choose the appropriate coordinate direction from the drop-down list.
     - Two Joints  option. When this option is selected, the lower portion of the form will display a Two Joints for Axial Reference Vector area with Axial Joint 1 and Axial Joint 2 drop-down lists. The lists consist of the joints included in the model and a None selection. Choose the two joints to be used to specify the axial reference vector.
     - User Vector  option. When this option is selected, the form will display a Coordinate System drop-down list and a User Axial Reference Vector area with edit boxes for Axial Vector X, Axial Vector Y, and Axial Vector Z. Select the coordinate system and then enter coordinate values in the edit boxes to specify the axial reference vector.
   - Plane Reference Vector Specified by  option. Choose one of the following options to specify how the plane reference vector will be specified:
   - - Coordinate Direction  option. When this option is selected, the  form will display a Coordinate System drop-down list and a Plane Coordinate Direction area with Primary and Secondary Dir (Direction) drop-down lists. Select the coordinate system for the reference vector and then choose a coordinate direction from each drop-down list.
     - Two Joints  option. When this option is selected, the lower portion of the form will display a Two Joints for Plane Reference Vector area with Plane Joint 1 and Plane Joint 2 drop-down lists. The lists consist of the joints included in the model and a None selection. Choose the two joints to be used to specify the plane reference vector.
     - User Vector  option. When this option is selected, the form will display a Coordinate System drop-down list and a User Plane Reference Vector area with edit boxes for Plane Vector X, Plane Vector Y, and Plane Vector Z. Select the coordinate system and then enter coordinate values in the edit boxes to specify the plane reference vector.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Assign/Solid/Solid_Material_Temperature.htm | Solid Material Temperature -->

# Solid - Material Temperature

Form:  Solid Material Temperature

Each solid object can be assigned an element material temperature. This is the temperature at which temperature-dependent properties are evaluated for the element.

1. Define a material property with temperature-dependent properties.
2. Use that material property in a [solid property definition](../../Define/Section_Properties/Solid_Property/Define_Solid_Property.md) and then [assign that property definition](Solid_Properties.md) to a [solid object](../../Edit/Extrude.md)(s).
3. Select the solid objects to be assigned a material temperature.
4. Click the Assign menu > Solid > Material Temperature command to access the Solid Material Temperature form. The material temperature can be a uniform temperature for the element or an average of the temperature for the joints as applied using a joint pattern.

   - Temperature option. Enter a temperature value in the Temperature edit box to specify a uniform temperature for the element. Be sure that the Joint Pattern drop-down list is blank.
   - Joint Pattern drop-down list. Enter a temperature value in the Temperature edit box and then select the [joint pattern](../Assign_Joint_Patterns.md). With this option SAP2000 uses a uniform temperature that is the average of the joint values.

The properties at this fixed temperature are used for all analyses regardless of any temperature changes experienced by the element during [loading](../Solid_Loads/Solid_Loads_Temperature.md).

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

# Solid - Properties

Form:  Solid Properties

Use the Assign menu > Solid > Properties command to assign [previously defined solid properties](../../Define/Section_Properties/Solid_Property/Define_Solid_Property.md) to selected solid objects.

1. Select one or more [solid objects](../../Edit/Extrude.md) to be assigned solid properties.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid > Properties command to access the Solid Properties form.
3. Select a previously defined solid property from the Properties list. Alternatively use the buttons on the form to add, modify, or delete a solid property definition before selecting a property for assignment. A description of those buttons is provided in the [Define Solid Property](../../Define/Section_Properties/Solid_Property/Define_Solid_Property.md) topic.
4. Click the OK button.

The assignments will be shown on the selected members on the main screen. Use the Assign menu > Clear Display of Assigns command to remove the display of assignments from the model.

See Also

<!-- source: Menus/Assign/Solid/Solid_Surface_Spring.htm | Solid Surface Spring -->

# Solid - Surface Spring

Form:  Assign Springs to Solid Object Face

Use the Assign menu > Solid > Surface Spring command to access the Assign Spring to Solid Object Face form and assign solid surface springs to selected solid objects. Solid surface springs can be assigned on any face of the solid object.

1. Select the [solid object(s)](../../Edit/Extrude.md) to be assigned surface springs.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid > Surface Spring command to access the Assign Spring to Solid Object Face form.

1. - Spring Type.
   - - Simple. When this option is selected, use the default value for the stiffness per unit area or enter another value in the Spring Stiffness per Unit Area edit box. Also specify if the spring has both Tension and Compression, or only Tension or only Compression by selecting the appropriate option from the Simple Spring Resists drop-down list.
     - Link Property. When this option is selected, the spring is a based on a link property. The option will be available if link properties have already been defined in the model; in that case, select the property from the drop-down list. If no link property has been defined, clicking the + (plus) symbol beside the drop-down list will access the [Link/Support Properties form](../../Define/Section_Properties/Link_Support_Properties/Define_Link_Support_Properties.md), which can be used to define the necessary link property. Then select that property in the drop-down list.
     - - Link Local 2-Axis Angle from Default Orientation edit box. This edit box becomes available when the spring is being defined using a link property definition. Use the edit box to specify an orientation angle for the link local axis measured counterclockwise from its default orientation.

1. - Solid Object Face drop-down list. Use this drop-down list to specify the [face](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Sign_Convention.md) to which the surface spring is being assigned.
   - Spring Tension Direction. Specify the direction of the spring tension, or when the Spring Type is Link Property, the direction of the spring, positive local 1-axis:
   - - Parallel to Solid Object Local Axis option and drop-down list. With this option, use the drop-down list to choose the local axis direction of the solid object in the model to which the spring is being assigned. The direction of the spring tension will be parallel to the selected local axis direction.
     - Normal to Specified Solid Object Face option and drop-down list. Specify that the spring tension direction be normal to a face of the solid object. Use the drop-down list to specify that the tension be inward or outward.
     - User Specified Direction Vector option and Coordinate System drop-down list and Global X, Y and Z Component edit boxes. Use this option to specify the spring tension direction along a specified vector. Select the Coordinate System for the vector from the drop-down list. The possible options include the Global axis, any [user-defined coordinate systems](../../Define/Coordinate_Grid_System/Define_Coordinate_Systems_Grid.md), and the local axes of the line object to which the spring is assigned.

1. - Options. Specify how the springs are to be assigned.
   - Add to Existing Springs option. Adds this assignment to the existing spring assignment(s).
   - Replace Existing Springs option. Replaces the existing spring assignment(s) with this new assignment. If no assignment exists, a new assignment is made. This is the default option.
   - Delete Existing Springs option. Deletes all surface spring assignments made to the selected solid object.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

[Solid - Switch Faces](Solid_Switch_Faces.md)

# Solid - Switch Faces

Form:  Modify Solid Face

The faces of a solid can be switched using the Assign menu > Solid > Switch Faces command.

1. Select the [solid object](../../Edit/Extrude.md) whose faces are to be switched.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid > Switch Faces command to display the Modify Solid Face form.

   - Switch Face drop-down list. Select the [face](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Sign_Convention.md) that is to be switched.
   - With Face drop-down list. Select the "new" face.
   - Options. Select how assignments to the face will be treated:
   - - Move Assignment with Face option.  Moves all the properties previously assigned to the face to the new location.
     - Do not Move Assignment with Face option. Moves the faces of the selected solid objects to their new locations but retains the assignments at the original positions.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Assign/Solid_Loads/Solid_Loads_Gravity.htm | Solid Loads Gravity -->

# Solid Loads - Gravity

Form:  Solid Gravity Loads

This loading method is a way to add the factored self weight of the objects as a force in any of the global directions. It is recommended that the actual self weight of the structure be included in the definition of the [static load pattern](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md). The load is calculated based on the mass density of the material used to define the material assigned to the corresponding section.

1. Select one or more [solids](../../Edit/Extrude.md) to be assigned loads.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid Loads > Gravity command to access the Solid Gravity Loads form.

   - Load Pattern Name drop-down list. Select the load pattern to which the gravity load is being added. Alternatively, click the + (plus symbol) beside the drop-down list to access the [Define Load Patterns form](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md); use the form to define a load pattern that will then be available in the drop-down list.
   - Gravity Multipliers edit boxes. Provide gravity multipliers in the specified global directions.
   - Coordinate System drop-down list. Select the coordinate system for the load from the drop-down list.
   - Options. Specify how the load is to be applied.
   - Add to Existing Loads option. Adds the specified load to the selected solid object. If one or more gravity load assignments have already been made, this option increases the load assuming, of course, that a positive load is being specified.
   - Replace Existing Loads option. Replaces the currently specified gravity load, if any, with the new load. If no assignment exists, a new assignment is made. This is the default option.
   - Delete Existing Loads option. Deletes any and all gravity load assignments made to the selected solid object. When this option is selected, the items in the Gravity Multiplier area of the form are ignored when the OK button is clicked.
   - Click the OK button.

The window will refresh with a graphical representation of the load assigned on the selected members. If necessary, use the Assign menu > Clear Assigns command to remove the display of the assigned load.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

# Solid Loads - Pore Pressure

Form:  Solid Pore Pressure Load

Pore pressure loads are used to model the drag and buoyancy effects of a fluid within a solid medium.

1. Select one or more [solids](../../Edit/Extrude.md) to be assigned loads.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid Loads > Pore Pressure command to access the Solid Pore Pressure Load form.

   - Load Pattern Name drop-down list. Select the load pattern to which the load is being assigned. Alternatively, click the + (plus symbol) beside the drop-down list to access the [Define Load Patterns form](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md); use the form to define a load pattern that will then be available in the drop-down list.
   - Pressure options. Choose if the pressure is to be applied by element or by joint pattern.

1. - - If by element, specify the pressure value.
     - If by [Joint Pattern](../Assign_Joint_Patterns.md), choose the pattern and specify the multiplier.
   - Options. Specify how the load is to be applied.

1. 1. - Add to Existing Loads option. Adds the specified pressure load to the solid object. If one or more pressure load assignments have already been made, this option increases the existing load, assuming a positive load is being specified.
      - Replace Existing Loads option. Replaces the currently specified pressure load, if any, with the new load. If no assignment exists, the new assignment is still made. This is the default option.
      - Delete Existing Loads option. Deletes any and all pressure load assignments made to the selected object(s). When this option is selected, the items in the Pressure area of the form are ignored when the OK button is clicked.

The window will refresh with a graphical representation of the load assigned on the selected members. If necessary, use the Assign menu > Clear Assigns command to remove the display of the assigned load.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

# Solid Loads - Strain

Form: Solid Strain Loads

Use the Assign menu > Solid Loads > Strain command to display the Solid Strain Loads form and specify the strain load on the selected solid object.

1. Select a solid object to be assigned the strain load.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid Loads > Strain command to display the Solid Strain Loads form.
3. Use the options on the form to specify the strain.

1. - Load Pattern Name drop-down list. Select the load pattern to which this strain load is to be added. Alternatively, click the + (plus symbol) beside the drop-down list to access the [Define Load Patterns form](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md); use the form to define a load pattern that will then be available in the drop-down list.
   - Units drop-down list. Use the units in this drop-down list or choose revised units for the form.
   - Strain Load options
   - - By Objects option. If this option is chosen, specify the strain value in the Strain edit box.
     - By Joint Pattern option. If this option is used, choose the [pattern](../Assign_Joint_Patterns.md) from the Pattern drop-down list and specify the multiplier in the Multiplier edit box.
   - Options. Specify how the load will be applied.
   - - Add to Existing Loads option. Adds the specified strain to the solid object. If one or more strain assignments have already been made, this option increases the existing strain.
     - Replace Existing Loads option.  Replaces the currently specified strain if any, with the new assignment. If no assignment exists, the new assignment is still made. This is the default option.
     - Delete Existing Loads option.  Deletes any and all strain assignments made to the selected joint(s). When this option is selected, the items in the Strain Load area of the form are ignored when the OK button is clicked.

The window will refresh with a graphical representation of the load assigned on the selected members. If necessary, use the Assign menu > Clear Assigns command to remove the display of the assigned load.

# Solid Loads - Surface Pressure

Form:  Solid Surface Pressure Load

Surface pressure always acts normal to the [element face](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Sign_Convention.md). Positive pressures are directed towards the interior of the element. The pressure may be constant over the face or interpolated from values given at the joints. The values at the joints are obtained from Joint Patterns, and need not be the same for different faces. Joint Patterns can be used to easily apply hydrostatic pressure.

1. Select one or more solids to be assigned loads.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid Loads > Surface Pressure command to access the Solid Surface Pressure Load form.

   - Load Pattern Name drop-down list. Select the load pattern to which the load is being assigned. Alternatively, click the + (plus symbol) beside the drop-down list to access the [Define Load Patterns form](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md); use the form to define a load pattern that will then be available in the drop-down list.
   - Pressure options. Choose if the pressure is to be applied by element or by joint pattern
   - - If by element, specify the pressure value.
     - If by [Joint Pattern](../Assign_Joint_Patterns.md), choose the pattern and specify the multiplier.
   - Option. Specify how the load is to be applied.
   - - Add to Existing Loads option. Adds the specified pressure load to the solid object. If one or more pressure load assignments have already been made, this option increases the existing load, assuming a positive load is being specified.
     - Replace Existing Loads option. Replaces the currently specified pressure load, if any, with the new load. If no assignment exists, the new assignment is still made. This is the default option.
     - Delete Existing Loads option. Deletes any and all pressure load assignments made to the selected object(s). When this option is selected, the items in the Pressure area of the form are ignored when the OK button is clicked.

The window will refresh with a graphical representation of the load assigned on the selected members. If necessary, use the Assign menu > Clear Assigns command to remove the display of the assigned load.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

# Solid Loads - Temperature

Form:  Solid Temperature Loading

The temperature load creates thermal strain in the solid element. This strain is given by the product of the material coefficient of thermal expansion and the temperature change of the object, which is the temperature being specified here.

1. Select one or more solids to be assigned a temperature load.
2. Click the Assign menu > Solid Loads > Temperature command to access the Solid Temperature Loading form.

   - Load Pattern Name drop-down list. Select the load pattern  to which the load is being assigned. Alternatively, click the + (plus symbol) beside the drop-down list to access the [Define Load Patterns form](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md); use the form to define a load pattern that will then be available in the drop-down list.
   - Temperature options. Choose if the temperature is to be applied by element or by joint pattern.
   - - If by element, specify the temperature value.
     - If by [Joint Pattern](../Assign_Joint_Patterns.md), choose the pattern and multiplier.
   - Option. Specify how the load is to be applied.
   - - Add to Existing Loads options. Adds the specified temperature load to the solid object. If one or more temperature load assignments have already been made, this option increases the existing load, assuming a positive load is being specified.
     - Replace Existing Loads options. Replaces the currently specified temperature load, if any, with the new load. If no assignment exists, the new assignment is still made. This is the default option.
     - Delete Existing Loads options. Deletes any and all temperature load assignments made to the selected object(s). When this option is selected, the items in the Temperature area of the form are ignored when the OK button is clicked.

The window will refresh with a graphical representation of the load assigned on the selected members. If necessary, use the Assign menu > Clear Assigns command to remove the display of the assigned load.

See Also

[Display - Show Miscellaneous Assigns - Solid](../../Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Solid.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Assign/Takeda_Hysteresis_Model.htm | Takeda Hysteresis Model -->

# Takeda Hysteresis Model

This model is very similar to the kinematic model, but uses a degrading hysteretic loop based on the Takeda model, as described in Takeda, Sozen, and Nielsen (1970). This simple model requires no additional parameters, and is more appropriate for reinforced concrete than for metals. Less energy is dissipated than for the kinematic model.

Unloading is along the elastic segments similar to the kinematic model. When reloading, the curve follows a secant line to the backbone curve for loading in the opposite direction. The target point for this secant is at the maximum deformation that occurred in that direction under previous load cycles. This results in a decreasing amount of energy dissipation with larger deformations. Unloading is along the elastic segments.

This behavior is illustrated in the figure.

![](../../assets/images/Hyst%20Takeda.bmp)

See Also:

[Hysteresis Types](Hysteresis_Types.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Assign/Tendon/Tendon_Local_Axes.htm | Tendon Local Axes -->

# Tendon - Local Axes

Form: Tendon Local Axis

The program automatically determines the local axis for  tendons from their connectivity and orientation.  The Assign > Tendon > Local Axis command can be used to modify these axes when necessary.

1. Select one or more tendons to be assigned a modified local axes.
2. Click the Assign menu > Tendon > Local Axes command to access the Tendon Local Axis form.
3. Type a value in the Angle in Degrees edit box. This is an angle by which local axis 2 of the object will be rotated around the local axis 1. Local axis 1 is along the length of the object. By default local axis 2 is always in the 1-Z plane, except if the object is vertical and then it is parallel to the global X axis. The definition of the local axes follows the right-hand rule. The angle is measured counter-clockwise as positive if the local axis 1 is pointing towards you.

Note:  By default global Z is taken as the 3D View Up Direction. If needed, change the UP direction for the display using the Options menu > 3D View Up Direction command. If the UP direction is changed, it will only affect the display of the model and does not affect the local axes definition in any way.

See Also

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Assign/Tendon/Tendon_Material_Temperature.htm | Tendon Material Temperature -->

# Tendon - Material Temperature

Form:  Tendon Material Temperature

The material temperature is the temperature at which temperature-dependent properties are evaluated for the object. The properties at this fixed temperature are used for all analyses, regardless of any temperature changes experienced by the object during loading. The object  material temperatures are (a) interpolated over an object from values given over joints, or (b) considered as uniform.

1. Select the objects to be assigned a material temperature.
2. Use the Assign menu > Tendon > Material Temperature command to access the Tendon Material Temperature form. The material temperature can be a uniform temperature for the object or an average of the temperature for the joints as applied using a joint pattern.

   - Temperature. Enter a temperature value in the Temperature edit box to specify a uniform temperature for the object. Be sure that the Joint Pattern drop-down list is blank.
   - Joint Pattern drop-down list. Enter a temperature value in the Temperature edit box and then select the [joint pattern](../Assign_Joint_Patterns.md). With this option SAP2000 uses a uniform temperature that is the average of the joint values.

The properties at this fixed temperature are used for all analyses regardless of any temperature changes experienced by the object during [loading](../Fame_Loads/Frame_Loads_Temperature.md).

Also see

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

# Tendon - Tension/Compression Limits

Form:  Tendon T/C Limits

An upper limit on the amount of tension and compression force supported by a [tendon object](../../Draw/Draw_Frame_Cable_Tendon.md) can be assigned. The behavior modeled is nonlinear but elastic. For example, assume a compression limit of zero has been set. If the object tries to go into axial compression, it will shorten without any stiffness. If the load reverses, it will recover its shortening with no stiffness, then engage with full stiffness when it reaches its original length.

1. Select the tendon(s) to be assigned axial force limits.
2. Use the Assign menu >Tendon > Tension/Compression Limits to access the  Tendon T/C Limits form:

1. - Tension Limit. Specify a tension limit by checking the Tension Limit box and entering a value that is zero or positive.
   - Compression Limit. Specify a compression limit by checking the Compression Limit box and entering a value that is zero or negative.

Note: If zero is specified for both the tension and compression limit, the object will carry no force in a nonlinear analysis.

|  |  |
| --- | --- |
| Note: | Tension/Compression limits are nonlinear. Thus, the following apply: |
|  | - Tension/compression limits will be activated in a nonlinear static or nonlinear direct-integration time-history analysis only. In general, use nonlinear analysis when tension/compression limits are present in the model. - If a linear analysis is performed using the stiffness at zero, the full axial stiffness (AE/L) of the element will be used as if there were no limits. - If a linear analysis is performed using the stiffness at the end of a nonlinear analysis, the axial stiffness will be zero or AE/L, depending on whether the object exceeded its limits at the end of the nonlinear case. |

Tip: This feature is useful for modeling cables and braces that can reasonably be represented by a single straight object when the analysis is focused more on the effect of the cable/brace on the structure than on the detailed behavior of the cable/brace itself.  
  
To model the deformation of the cable or brace in detail, [break the cable/brace into several sub-objects,](../../Draw/Curved_Frames_and_Cables/Cable_Geometry_Form.md) and use large-displacements analysis without compression limits. Under compression, the cable/brace will buckle out of the way in a more realistic representation of the true behavior.

See Also

[Selection List](../../../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Selection_List.md)

# Tendon Loads - Gravity

Form: Tendon Gravity Loads

This loading method is a way to add the factored self weight of the members as a force in any of the global directions. It is recommended that the actual self weight of the structure be included in the definition of the [static load pattern](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md).

1. Select one or more tendons to be assigned gravity load.
2. Click the Assign menu > Tendon Loads > Gravity command to access the Tendon Gravity Loads form.

   - Load Pattern Name drop-down list. Select the load pattern to which the load is being added. Alternatively, click the + (plus symbol) beside the drop-down list to access the [Define Load Patterns form](../../Define/Load_Pattern/Define_Load_Patterns.md); use the form to define a load pattern that will then be available in the drop-down list.
   - Gravity Multipliers edit boxes. Provide values for gravity multipliers in the Global X, Y and Z directions.
   - Coordinate System drop-down list. Select the coordinate system in which the load will be applied from the drop-down list.
   - Options. Specify how the load will be applied.

1. 1. - Add to Existing Loads: Adds the specified gravity load to the selected object. If one or more gravity load assignments have already been made, this option increases the existing load, assuming a positive load is being specified.
      - Replace Existing Loads: Replaces the currently specified gravity load, if any, with the new load. If no assignment exists, the new assignment is still made. This is the default option.
   1. - Delete Existing Loads: Deletes any and all gravity load assignments made to the selected object(s). When this option is selected, the items in the Gravity Multipliers area of the form are ignored when the OK button is clicked.

The window will refresh with a graphical representation of the load assigned on the members selected.

# Advanced Foundation Property

Use the Advanced Foundation Properties form to select the advanced foundation type to be defined. There are five advanced foundation types available:

- Isolated Footing
- Combined Footing
- Pile Group
- Pile Pier
- Pile Shaft

After selecting the type, use the Foundation Property Data form to specify the appropriate parameters that define the geometry, materials, soil properties, and other characteristics of the foundation.

The Combined Footing is considered a strip-type foundation and may connect to more than one point along a line. The remaining types are considered isolated foundations, which connect to a single point.

Once a foundation property is defined, it can be used to draw foundation assemblies, which are parametrically generated collections of component objects (points, lines, areas, and links). Use the Draw > Isolated Foundation or Draw > Strip Foundation command, depending on the type of foundation property. For isolated-type foundations, clicking a single control point will generate a foundation assembly below the control point. For strip-type foundations, clicking two control points will generate a foundation assembly below the two control points; intermediate points may be connected as an option.

|  |
| --- |
| Access the Advanced Foundation Property form as follows:  *Click the Define > Foundation Properties menu to display the Define Foundation Properties form. Then click the Add New Foundation button to display the Advanced Foundation Properties form.* |

## See Also

[Define Foundation Properties](Define_Foundation_Properties_form_-_For_SAP2000.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Combined_Footing_Foundation_Property.htm | Combined Footing Foundation Property -->

# **Combined Footing Foundation Property**

Use the Combined Footing Foundation form to define the material, dimensions and soil properties for a combined footing foundation property. This property can be assigned to a pair of joints using the Draw > Strip Foundation command.

The combined footing will be modeled as area objects at the mid-surface of the footing. All the footing area objects are assigned with compression-only area spring at the bottom face of each area object to provide the vertical support. The spring constant is the average soil modulus within the thickness of the footing. For the area objects with edges on the edges of the footing, additional area edge springs with the same spring constant will be assigned to these area objects to provide the horizontal support. If the depth of the footing exceeds the depth of the specified soil layers, then the property from the deepest soil layer will be used for the exceeding depth of the footing.

After this property is assigned to joints, the top of the footing will be located at the same elevation as the average of the assigned joints. The footing is extended as needed to accommodate the assigned columns plus the specified cantilever distances. The top point of the footing under the first column is called the insertion point. In the model, the frame members will be extended to the mid-surface of the footing area objects, and assigned corresponding end offsets with rigid zone factor 0.5.

Note: It is important that all the columns assigned to the same combined footing have the same bottom elevation. Otherwise, some or all of the columns may not connect to the footing.

- **General:**
- - **Name: The name of the foundation property.**
- **Footing:**
- - **Footing Material: Specify a previously defined material for the combined footing.**
  - **Total Width, Ly: The width of the footing transverse to the line connecting the two joints that define the combined footing (footing Y-axis).**
  - Left Cantilever, L1: The length of the left cantilever of the combined footing measured from the left edge of the footing to the center of the left most (first) column.
  - **Right Cantilever, L2:** The length of the right cantilever of the combined footing measured from the right edge of the footing to the center of the right most (last) column.
  - **Thickness, T: The thickness of the combined footing.**
  - **Max. Mesh Size: The maximum area-object mesh size for the combined footing model.**
- **Soil Properties:**
- - **Soil Cover, Sc: The distance above the top surface of the footing to the top of soil, where soil layers start.**
  - **Layer Properties: The values of the modulus of subgrade reaction in the soil layers. To edit these values, click the item “Layer Properties” and then click the “…” button. This will display the** **[Soil Layer Properties](Soil_Layer_Properties.md)** **form.**
- **Model 3D:**
- - **Use the controls in this region to control the 3D display of the defined foundation property.**

|  |
| --- |
| Access the Combined Footing Foundation Property form as follows:   1. Click the Define > Foundation Properties command to bring up the [Advanced Foundation Properties](Advanced_Foundation_Property_-_For_SAP2000.md) form. 2. Click the Add New Foundation button to display the  Add Foundation Property form. Then click the Advanced Foundation Properties form, select  Combined Footing and click OK.  Alternatively, highlight the name of a previously defined foundation in the Foundation area and click the Add Copy of Foundation or Modify/Show Foundation button to display the Combined Footing Foundation Property form. |

## See Also

## [Draw Strip Foundation](../Draw/Draw_Strip_Foundation.md)

# Coordinate System Location and Orientation Form

Use options on the Coordinate System Location and Orientation form to locate the origin of the coordinate system for a model. The values specified on the form are offsets from the global coordinate system, which has its origin at 0, 0, 0.

- System Name display box. The name of the system being located relative to the global coordinate system is displayed here.
- 2-D or 3-D option. Select 2-D if the new system differs from the Global system only in the X-Y plane. Select 3-D if a more general 3-D transformation is required. The option selected determines the data required in the other areas of the form.
- Origin Location - Enter the location of the origin of the new system, given in Global coordinates:
- - For 2-D systems, enter only the global X and Y coordinates. The Z coordinate is taken to be zero.
  - For 3-D systems, enter the global X, Y, and Z coordinates of the origin of the new system.

If all three coordinates are set to zero, the system has the same origin as the Global system.

- Origin Orientation - Rotations in Degrees - Enter the angles, in degrees, that define how the axes of the new system are rotated with respect to the Global system.

For 2-D systems, specify only the rotation about the Z axis. This is the angle from the Global X axis to the new X axis, measured counter-clockwise in the X-Y plane.

For 3-D systems, specify the three rotations that are applied in the following sequence:

1. - First, rotate the new system about its Z axis, which is currently parallel to the Global Z axis.
   - Next, rotate the new system about its resulting Y axis, which is currently parallel to the Global X-Y plane, but not necessarily parallel to the Global Y axis.
   - Finally, rotate the new system about its resulting X axis.

Any coordinate system orientation can be described by means of these three angles. The order of application is important. If all three angles are set to zero, the system has the same orientation as the Global system.

|  |
| --- |
| Access the Coordinate System Location and Orientation form as follows:  Method 1:   1. Click the File menu > New Model to display the New Model form. 2. Choose a template to display the {Template} form. Then do one of the following:     - Check the Use Custom Grid Spacing and Locate Origin check box and click the Edit Grid button to display the Define Grid Data form. On that form click the  Locate System Origin button.    - Click the  Locate Origin button on the selected {Template} form.   Method 2   1. Click the Define menu > Coordinate Systems/Grids command to display the Coordinate/Grid Systems form. 2. Use one of the following:     - Click the Add New System button.    - Highlight a previously defined [Regular System](Define_Coordinate_Systems_Grid.md) definition and click the Add Copy of System or Modify/Show System button to display the Define Grid Data form. On that form, click the  Locate System Origin button.    - Highlight a previously defined [General System](Define_Coordinate_Systems_Grid.md) and click the Add Copy of System or Modify/Show System button to display the Grid System Data form.  On that form, click the Coordinate System button. |

# Define Coordinate Systems/Grids

Form: Coordinate/Grid Systems

Use the Define menu > Coordinate System/Grids command to access the Coordinate/Grid Systems form. Alternatively, right click in a blank area of a display window showing an undeformed shape and select the Edit Grid Data command from the resulting pop-up menu to access the form. Use the Coordinate/Grid Systems form to (a) access other forms that can be used to add a new coordinate system and uniform grid, (b) convert a previously defined [uniform (regular) grid system](Quick_Grid_Lines_Form.md) to a [general (non-uniform) grid system](Grid_System_Data_Form.md), or (c) delete a previously defined coordinate/grid system.

Coordinate systems are defined by specifying their origins and orientations with respect to the fixed Global coordinate system. They are used to define the location and orientation of the associated grid system. Thus, coordinate systems are always defined as part of a coordinate/grid system pair. However, when only a coordinate system is needed, such as when viewing the model, defining the model (object local axes, loads, and the like), and reporting results, a coordinate/grid system can be defined with no grid lines.

A grid system is a set of intersecting lines used to aid in drawing the model. Grid systems may be Cartesian (rectangular), cylindrical, or general. Each grid system is defined with respect to its own coordinate system, so, as indicated previously, grid and coordinate systems are defined together as a single entity. An unlimited number of coordinate/grid systems can be defined, each with a unique name.

A regular system is any coordinate/grid system having a Cartesian (rectangular) or cylindrical grid system. A general system is a system comprised of arbitrarily defined grid lines. The Define Grid Data form can be used to define a regular system. To determine if a previously defined system is a regular or general system, access the Coordinate/Grid Systems form and highlight the system name in the Systems display area. If the Convert to General Grid check box is NOT checked (with the system name highlighted), the grid system is a regular system.

The Global coordinate system always exists, and has its own grid. All other systems are user defined with respect to the Global system.

Note:  Right clicking anywhere in an active window will display a drop-down menu of commands, including the Edit Grid Data command. Clicking that command will display the Coordinate/Grid Systems form.

Use the following buttons and option on the Coordinate/Grid Systems form to define a new coordinate/grid system:

- Add New System button.

Define a regular system as follows:

1. 1. Click the Add New System button to access the Coord System Location and Orientation form.
   2. Make any adjustment to the system location and orientation.
   3. Click the OK button to access the [Define Grid System Data form](Define_Grid_System_Data_Form.md); use that form to define the grid system.

Define a general system as follows:

- 1. Define a regular system using the Coord System Location and Orientation and Define Grid System Data forms as described above, except it is not necessary to define the grid system at this point.
  2. Click the OK button on the Define Grid Data form to redisplay the Coordinate/Grid Systems form and highlight the name of the new system in the Systems display list.
  3. Check the Convert to General Grid check box. The selected system will be instantly converted from a regular system (Cartesian or cylindrical)  to an equivalent general type.
- Add Copy of System button.
- 1. Click on a previously named system in the Systems display area to select it.
  2. Click the Add Copy of System button to access the Define Grid System Data form if a  regular system was highlighted or the Grid System Data form if a general system was highlighted; make any necessary modifications and click the OK button. SAP2000 will add a new coordinate/grid system that is identical to the selected system. The name of the system will be the same as the original system with a -1 added; for example, if the system being copied is CSYS1, the duplicate name will be CSYS1-1.
- Modify/Show System button.
- 1. Click on an existing Coordinate/Grid system to select it
  2. Click the Modify/Show System button to access the Define Grid System Data form (a regular system) or the [Grid System Data form](Grid_System_Data_Form.md) (a general system).
  3. Use the form to modify the grid system.
- Delete System button.
- 1. Click on a previously defined system in the Systems display area to select it.
  2. Click the Delete System button to delete the selected system.

Any coordinates defined with respect to the deleted system will be converted to global coordinates. If a system selected to be deleted is in use as part of some other definition in the model, it cannot be deleted.

- Convert to General Grid check box.
- Click on a system in the Systems display area to select it. If the Convert to General Grid check box is checked, the selected system is a general system (not Cartesian or cylindrical) and it cannot be changed to a regular system (Cartesian or cylindrical).
- If the Convert to General Grid check box is unchecked, the selected system is a regular system.
- Check the check box to instantly convert a selected uniform system to an equivalent general type system. After a system has been converted to a general system, it cannot be changed back to a uniform system. If the check box is checked by accident, click the Cancel button to exit the form without saving any changes.

Example:  Definition of a coordinate system/grid is demonstrated in [Problem A](../../../Example_Problems/Problem_A.md), [Problem C](../../../Example_Problems/Problem_C.md), [Problem V](../../../Example_Problems/Problem_V.md),  and [Problem Z](../../../Example_Problems/Problem_Z.md).

# Define Grid System Data Form

For a regular or general system, the coordinate system is defined using an origin and orientation relative to the Global coordinate system. All coordinate systems follow the right-hand rule. The grid lines for a regular system are defined relative to X, Y, or Z (Cartesian) or r, theta, or Z (cylindrical). The grid lines for a general system are defined relative to XY and Z only.

- Display Grid as:  Ordinates or Spacing. Choose to display the locations of the points defining the grid line using coordinates or lengths in the current units relative to the origin. The ordinates or the spacing will display in the X/R, Y/Theta, and Z Grid Data spreadsheets (Regular System) or the Z Grid Data spreadsheet (General System).
- X/R Grid Data, Y/Theta Grid Data, and Z Grid Data spreadsheets for a Regular System or Z Grid Data spreadsheet for a General System.
- - Quick Start button. This spreadsheet area will be empty if the form is accessed after the model has been started (i.e., if Method 2 for a regular system or 2.a for a general system, above, was used to access this form). Click this button to access the [Quick Grid Lines form](Quick_Grid_Lines_Form.md) and specify the number of grid lines, the grid spacing, and the coordinates of the first grid line location to quickly define a grid system. The grid data will be transferred to the spreadsheet automatically when the OK button is clicked on the Quick Grid Lines form. The program will apply default IDs, Line Types, and so forth, that can then be modified as needed.
  - Grid ID column. This column displays the identification number for the grid lines in the coordinate system. If needed, click in the cell and type in a new ID.
  - Ordinate/Spacing column. Use the cells in this column to specify the location of the end point for the grid line relative to the origin of the coordinate system.
  - Line Type column. The grid line can be a primary or secondary line. Click in the cell to choose the appropriate option.
  - Visibility column. Use this column to specify that the grid line be visible or invisible. Click in the cell to choose the appropriate option.
  - Bubble Loc column. By default, the ID bubble for the X grid displays at the End of the grid line, the bubble for the Y grid displays at the Start of the grid line, and the bubble for the Z grid displays at the End of the grid line. Click in the cells in this column and select the appropriate option to reverse the location of the ID bubble.
  - Grid Color column. Use the cells in this column to specify the display color for the grid line. Double click on the cell to display the Color form and select a new color.
  - Edit menu. Use the commands on the form's Edit menu to Cut, Copy, Paste, and Delete the data in the spreadsheet area. Highlight a row of data before clicking the Edit menu > Insert Row or Edit menu > Delete Row commands to add or remove rows of data, respectively. Adding or removing rows adds or deletes grid lines.
  - Format menu. Use the form's Format menu to change the color for a selected row of data.
- Hide All Grid Lines check box. When this check box is checked, the grid lines will not display on the model.
- Glue to Grid Lines check box. Check the Glue to Grid Lines check box so that joints will move with the grids when the grid lines are moved. This is a very powerful way to quickly edit the structure without redefining joint locations.
- Bubble Size edit box. Use this edit box to specify the size of the ID bubble in pixels.
- Reset to Default Color button. Click this button to reset the display color for the grid line to the default setting. This button appears on the form only when the system is a Regular system.
- Reorder Ordinates button. This button is available when the Ordinates option is selected in the Display Grid as area of the form. Clicking this button will arrange the ordinates in sequential order.
- Locate System Origin button. Click this button to display the [Coord System Location and Orientation form](Coord_System_Location_and_Orientation_Form.md) and define a new coordinate system.

Then click the Add Copy of System or Modify/Show System button to display the Grid System Data form.  3. Click the Define Z Grid Lines button. |

# Grid Line Form

Use the Grid Line form
to specify the appearance and location of the selected grid line.

- Grid
  Line ID edit box. Use the default grid line name or type a
  new name in the edit box.
- Type
  of Grid Line options. Choose to specify the grid line as a
  Straight Line, or an Arc.
- Plan
  Coordinates, X1, Y1, X2, Y2, XC, YC
  edit boxes. Use these edit boxes to specify the location for the grid
  line.
- Primary
  Line or Secondary Line
  options. Choose to specify the grid line as a primary or secondary
  grid line.
- Hide
  Grid Line check box. When this check box is checked, the grid
  line will not display in the model.
- Switch Bubble Location check box.
  By default, the ID bubble for the X grid displays at the end of the
  grid line, the bubble for the Y grid displays at the start of the
  grid line, and the bubble for the Z grid displays at the end of the
  grid line. When this check box is checked, the ID bubble for the grid
  line will be displayed opposite to its default location (e.g., the
  X grid bubble will display at the start of the grid line).
- Bubble
  Size edit box. Use this edit box to specify the size of the
  ID bubble for the grid line in pixels.
- Color
  display box. This display box shows the color that will be used to
  display the grid lines. Click on the color to display the Color
  form and select another color.
- Apply
  to All check boxes. When any of these check boxes is checked,
  the associated parameter will be applied to all grid lines in the
  model not only the grid line specified in the Grid
  Line ID edit box.

# Grid System Data Form

Use the Grid System Data form to add, modify, or delete a grid line in Plan for a [general system](Define_Coordinate_Systems_Grid.md).

- Grid System edit box. The name displayed in this edit box is the name of the system specified using the Coordinate/Grid Systems form. This name can be changed by typing a revised name in the edit box.
- Grid Lines in Plan display area. This area of the form lists the grid lines comprising the grid system. The initial grid lines, if any, reflect the number of grid lines in the X and Y directions specified using the [Define Grid System Data form (i.e., before the regular system was converted to a general system).](Define_Grid_System_Data_Form.md)
- - Add New Grid Line button. Click this button to display the [Grid Line form](Grid_Line_Form.md) and specify the parameters to define a new grid line.
  - Add Modify/Show Grid Line button.
  1. 1. Highlight the ID of the grid line to be reviewed or modified in the Grid Lines in Plan display area.
     2. Click the Add Modify/Show Grid Line button to display the [Grid Line form](Grid_Line_Form.md).
     3. Use the form to modify the definition of the selected grid line, including the type of line (straight or arc), the X and Y coordinates for the grid line, bubble size, color and other items.
  - Delete Grid Line button.
  1. 1. Highlight the name of the grid line to be deleted in the Grid Lines in Plan display area.
     2. Click the Delete Grid Line button to delete the selected grid line.
- Define Z Grid Lines button. Click this button to display the [Define Grid System Data form and review or modify the parameters used to specify the display of the grid lines, including the ID, location, line type, color and label bubble.](Define_Grid_System_Data_Form.md)
- Coordinate System button. Click this button to display the [Coord System Location and Orientation form](Coord_System_Location_and_Orientation_Form.md) and define a new coordinate system.

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Coordinate_Grid_System/Quick_Grid_Lines_Form.htm | Quick Grid Lines Form -->

# Quick Grid Lines Form

A Cartesian (rectangular) or cylindrical grid system is a uniform system and is called a regular system. A system comprised of arbitrarily defined grid lines is a non-uniform system and is called a general system.

The Quick Grid Lines form can be used to define a regular system using the following tabs and edit boxes:

- Cartesian or Cylindrical tab. Click the appropriate tab to select the type of grid system being defined:
- - A Cartesian system has grid lines parallel to the X, Y, and Z axes of the grid coordinate system.
  - A cylindrical system has radial, circumferential, and axial grid lines. The radial and circumferential grid lines are parallel to the X-Y plane of the grid coordinate system. The axial grid lines are parallel to the Z axis of the grid coordinate system.
- System Name edit box. Enter the name of the grid system being defined. For a new model (i.e., Method 1 above for accessing the form), the grid system is being defined for the Global coordinate system, and the name cannot be changed.
- Number of Grid Lines edit boxes.  Enter the number of grid lines in each of the three directions.
- Grid Spacing edit boxes.  Enter the distance between grid lines in each of the three directions. Length units are used for all directions except for theta in cylindrical grids, which uses angles measured in degrees. The total length (or angle) in each direction is the product of the number of grid spaces and the distance between grid lines. A zero distance (or angle) is not allowed.
- First Grid Line Location edit boxes. Specify the X, Y and Z coordinates for the first grid lines in the X direction, Y direction and Z direction.

# Define Excitation Set

Form:  Define Excitation Set

You open this form using the Define menu > Floor Vibration > Excitation Set command. This form allows you to create, edit and delete Excitation Sets.

An Excitation Set refers to a set of input values required by the program for the analysis of floor vibrations in steel-framed structures. This set includes key information, such as the location of the vibration source and the location where the vibration's impact is measured. It also includes other parameters, like the damping value and the associated modal case.

For more information on Floor Vibration Analysis in Steel-Framed Structures refer to the the Technical Note on*Floor Vibration Analysis*.

## See Also

[Edit Excitation Set](Edit_Excitation_Form.md)

[Walking Vibration Analysis Form](../Display/Walking_Vibration_Analysis_Form.md)

# Define Foundation Properties Form

Form: Define Foundation Properties

Click the Define > Foundation Properties menu to display the Define Foundation Properties form, which is used to add, modify or delete foundation property definitions.

- Add New Foundation Property button. Click this button to display the Advanced Foundation Properties form.

  1. Select the type of foundation from one of the following templates: [Isolated Footing](Isolated_Footing_Foundation_Property.md), [Combined Footing](Combined_Footing_Foundation_Property.md), [Pile Group](Pile_Group_Foundation_Property.md), [Pile Pier](Pile_Pier_Foundation_Property.md), and [Pile Shaft](Pile_Shaft_Foundation_Property.md). The Combined Footing is a strip-type foundation, and the rest are isolated-type foundations.
  2. Specify the appropriate parameters that define the geometry, materials, soil properties, and other characteristics of the foundation on the Foundation Property Data form.
- Add Copy of Foundation button.

  1. Highlight the name of a previously defined foundation property.
  2. Click the Add Copy of Foundation button to display the Foundation Property Data form. The new foundation property will be of the same type as the source property.
  3. Make the necessary modification to the property definition. The type of foundation cannot be changed.
- Modify/Show Foundation button.

  1. Highlight the name of a previously defined foundation property.
  2. Click the Modify/Show Foundation button to display the Foundation Property Data form.
  3. Use the form to view or modify the definition. The type of foundation property cannot be changed.
- Delete Foundation button.

  1. Highlight the name of a previously defined foundation property.
  2. Click the Delete Foundation button to be delete the foundation property.

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Edit_Excitation_Form.htm | Edit Excitation Form -->

# Edit Excitation Form

Use the **Edit Excitation Form** to edit the parameters of the Excitation Sets that are used for the analysis of floor vibrations in steel-framed structures.

## General parameters

- **Excitation Type**  denotes the type of vibrations being analyzed. For example, vibrations induced due to walking or running and their impact on affected occupants or sensitive equipment resting on the floor.
- The **Excitation Joint** refers to the Label (SAP2000) or the Unique Name (ETABS) of a Joint Object located where the vibration originates.
- The **Response Joint** refers to the Label (SAP2000) or the Unique Name (ETABS) of a Joint Object located where the vibration's impact is measured.

Engineering judgment should be used to identify the Excitation and Response Joint locations. For example, for walking vibrations, it is recommended that an unobstructed walking path of approximately 15ft long that lies as close as possible to the maximum mode shape value should be identified. The Excitation Joint should be located near the midpoint of such a walking path. The Response Joint should be located at the affected occupant’s location. Note that it is possible for the Excitation Joint and the Response Joint to have the same location. Thus, they can be associated to the same Joint Object.

## Steady State Load Case Parameters

- Name of an existing Steady-State **Function** to apply the vibration-inducing load. It is recommended to use a unit uniform function, such as the program’s default function “UNIFSS”. SS-functions are defined in Define > Functions > Steady-State.
- **Modal Case**to be used in the steady-state load case.
- The **Damping**value specified in this Form refers to the stiffness proportional coefficient to be used in the modal damping of the Excitation Set’s steady-state load case. If the viscous damping ratio is known, it is recommended to use the following relation:

*d*

)*  is the stiffness proportional coefficient, and *ζ*  is the known viscous damping ratio.

- Last Frequency: The total frequency range for the analysis is from zero to the value specified as Last Frequency. A value of 20 Hz is recommended, as frequencies higher than 20 Hz are typically not relevant in the context of floor vibration analysis.

For more information on Floor Vibration Analysis in Steel-Framed Structures refer to the the Technical Note on*Floor Vibration Analysis*.

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Foundation_Assembly_Data_form_-_For_Both.htm | Foundation Assembly Data form -->

# Foundation Assembly Data Form

A foundation assembly is a parametrically generated collection of components objects (points, lines, areas, and links) intended to represent footings and pile groups, along with the associated soil properties. A foundation assembly will be regenerated whenever the parametric definition is changed. This includes changes made to the properties used by the parametric foundation, as well as geometrical changes to the control points.

To create a foundation assembly, first define a foundation property. Then use the Draw > Isolated Foundation or Draw > Strip Foundation command, depending on the type of foundation property. For isolated-type foundations, clicking a single control point will generate a foundation assembly below the control point. For strip-type foundations, clicking two control points will generate a foundation assembly below the two control points.

Once a foundation assembly has been generated, you can use the Foundation Assembly Data form to modify, update or unlink a parametric foundation assembly. The following parameters and operations are available:

- **Name** text box: The name of the foundation assembly. Changing the name does not require an update of the foundation assembly.
- **Property** text box: This is the foundation property name used to create the foundation assembly. This is for information only and cannot be changed once a foundation has been drawn.
- **Connection Point(s)** text box: This lists the points that are connected to the foundation assembly. These points include the control point or points used to draw the foundation, as well as any intermediate points that may be connected in the case of a strip-type foundation. This is for information only.
- **Rotation about Global Z** text box: This is the rotation angle about the global Z-axis for an isolated-type foundation, measured counterclockwise from the global X-axis to the x-axis of the foundation when looking down from above.
- **Include Intermediate Points** check box: Check this box to connect intermediate points located between the two control points of a strip-type foundations to the foundation assembly. Only point objects that lie on the straight line between the two control points will be connected. Points created for analysis by auto-meshing will not be automatically connected.
- **Update** button: Click this button to regenerate the parametric foundation assembly. This will delete the previously generated component objects (points, lines, areas, and links) and regenerate them based settings in this form. Any manual assignments or edits to the previous component objects will be lost. This cannot be undone.
- **Unlink** button: Click this button to delete the foundation assembly but keep the generated component objects and their assignments. This cannot be undone.

## **See Also**

[Advanced Foundation Property](Advanced_Foundation_Property_-_For_SAP2000.md)

[Foundation Assembly Operations](Foundation_Assembly_Operations_form_-_For_SAP2000.md)

Select the foundation assembly to display the Foundation Assembly Data form.   Alternatively, the Foundation Assembly Data form can be accessed by clicking the Modify/Show button in the Foundation Assembly Operations form (command Define > Foundation Assemblies). |

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Foundation_Assembly_Operations_form_-_For_SAP2000.htm | Foundation Assembly Operations form -->

# Foundation Assembly Operations Form

The Foundation Assembly Operations form is used operate on existing parametric foundation assemblies and is accessed by the menu command Define > Foundation Assemblies. The following operations can be performed.

- Modify/Show button: Highlight one of the foundation assemblies in the list and click this button to edit the foundation assembly name and its parameters. See the Foundation Assembly Data form for more information.
- Update button: Highlight the name of one or more foundation assemblies in the list and click this button to update the selected foundations. This will delete the previously generated component objects (points, lines, areas, and links) and regenerate them based upon the properties of each foundation assembly. Any manual assignments or edits to the previous component objects will be lost.
- Unlink button: Highlight the name of one or more foundation assemblies in the list and click this button to delete the selected foundation assembly definitions but keep the generated component objects. This cannot be undone, although you can re-create a foundation assembly using the appropriate Draw command.
- Delete button: Highlight the name of one or more foundation assemblies in the list and click this button to delete the selected foundation assemblies, including their generated component objects. This cannot be undone, although you can re-create a foundation assembly using the appropriate Draw command.
- Select Highlighted Foundation Assemblies check box: When this box is checked, the generated components for all the highlighted foundation assemblies will become selected in the model display windows. This selection is updated whenever different foundations are highlighted. Whatever selection is active when the Foundation Assembly Operations form is closed will remain. If this check box is not checked, the generated components are not selected for the highlighted foundation assemblies. Note that any previous selection of objects that are not part of foundation assemblies is not affected.

## See Also

[Advanced Foundation Property](Advanced_Foundation_Property_-_For_SAP2000.md)

[Define Foundation Properties](Define_Foundation_Properties_form_-_For_SAP2000.md)

[Foundation Assembly Data](Foundation_Assembly_Data_form_-_For_Both.md)

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Functions/Power_Spectral_Density/Define_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.htm | Define Power Spectral Density Function -->

# Define Power Spectral Density Function

Form:  Define Power Spectral Density Functions

Use the Define menu > Functions > Power
Spectral Density Functions command to access the Define
Power Spectral Density Functions form and add, modify, or delete
power spectral density functions. A power spectral density function is
a list of function values versus frequency of excitation. The function
values in a power-spectral-density function may refer to normalized ground
acceleration values or to multipliers for specified (force or displacement)
load patterns.

This is a probabilistic type of function. Function values are specified
as the square
of the input value per
unit of frequency. In other words, this function should be specified
so that the square-root of the integral of the function over the frequency
range gives the expected RMS (root-mean-square) magnitude of loading.
Function values may not be negative.

Note: By default,
the program pre-defines a unit constant power spectral density function.
This function may be modified or deleted.

Important:
You may define a power-spectral-density function for any frequency range
you want, f0 to fn.
For all frequencies less than the first given frequency f0,
the function value is assumed to be constant at the function value specified
for f0. For all frequencies greater
than the last given frequency fn,
the function value is assumed to be constant at the function value specified
for fn. If you want the function
value to be zero outside of a particular frequency range, you must define
the first and/or last function values to be zero.

Tip: The frequency
range may be specified in Hz (cycles per second) or RPM (cycles per minute).
Internally, the program always uses Hz, and results are reported in Hz.
The frequency unit also affects the function values, since they are specified
per frequency.

Use the buttons on the  Define Power Spectral
Density Functions form to add, modify, or delete power spectral
density functions as follows:

- Add
  New Function button.
- 1. Select Function
     from File or User Function
     from the Choose Function Type
     to Add drop-down list.
  2. Click the Add Function button to display the Power Spectral Density Function Definition
     form  ([Function
     from File](File_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.md) or [User
     Function](User_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.md) ). The appearance of, and options available on, the
     form depend on the option selected in Step 1.
- Modify/Show
  Function button.
- 1. Highlight a function
     definition in the Functions
     display area.
  2. Click the Modify/Show button to access the form for
     a [Function
     from File](File_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.md) or a [User
     Function](User_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.md), depending on the type of function selected in Step
     1. Note that the form for a Function from File has a button that
     can be used to change the function to a User Defined function.
- Delete
  Function button.
- 1. Highlight a function
     definition in the Functions display area.
  2. Click the Delete Function button to delete the selected
     function.  A function being used by an [load
     case](../../../Analyze/Set_Load_Cases_to_Run_and_Run_Analysis.md) can not be deleted.

Use the *Default Function Folder* area to browse for & set
the default folder to (recursively) search if a function data file is
not found in the specified path or in the model folder of a “From File” type function.

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Functions/Power_Spectral_Density/File_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.htm | File Power Spectral Density Function -->

# Function From File - Power Spectral Density Function

When defining a power spectral density function from file, the Power Spectral Density Function Definition form has the following areas:

- Function name edit box.  Specify the name of the function or use the default.
- Function File area.  Click the Browse button to display the Pick Function Data File form and select the name of the text file that includes the power spectral density function data. The name of the selected file will appear in the File Name display box. Click the View File button to display the selected file in text format in WordPad.

The File Name Loaded From display box shows the full path of the data file the program will use for plotting and analysis. This will be identical to File Name if the data file can be loaded from the specified path. If the data file is no longer found in the specified path, the program will recursively search the following locations in the order given below, and load & use the first matching data file:

1. 1. The specified full path in the function definition.
   2. Folder where the model file is saved.
   3. Default Function Folder specified in Define Power Spectral Density Functions form.
   4. Program installation folder.

Typically, the program does not import the file into its database. It simply maintains a link to the file location. Thus, if the power spectral density function file or the .SDB file is moved to another location, the program may be unable to locate the function file. If the Convert to User Defined button is clicked, the program imports the function into its database file and the data will always be available to the model. Do not click the Convert to User Defined button until all information in the Function File, Values are and Format Type areas has been specified.

- Header Lines to Skip edit box, Prefix Characters per Line to Skip edit box, and Number of Points per Line edit box. Note that when reading the function file, the program skips the number of lines at the top of the file indicated in the Header Lines to Skip edit box. It also skips the number of characters at the beginning of each line specified in the Prefix Characters per Line to Skip edit box. The Number of Points per Line edit box tells the program how many function values or pairs of frequency and function values are specified on each line. Additional data on each line will be ignored. Thus, the program reads the file as follows:

  1. 1. First, the program skips the specified number of header lines.
     2. Next, the program checks to see if a line has a $ symbol as the first character. If it does, the program skips to the next line.
     3. If a $ symbol is not the first character on the line, the program reads the information on the line, skipping the specified number of characters at the beginning of the line.
     4. If the line is blank or if the end of the file is reached, the program stops reading and closes the file.
- Values are area.  Specifies whether the text file contains pairs of Frequency and Function Values or Values at Equal Intervals of (i.e., function values that are spaced at equal frequency intervals). If the file contains only function values, specify the equal frequency interval.
- Format type options.  The format type can be specified as Free Format or Fixed Format. In free format, items on the lines can be separated by spaces or tabs. If the fixed format type is chosen, also specify the number of Characters per item. Each item on a line is assigned the same number of character spaces. The program begins counting the spaces after it skips the number of prefix characters specified in the Function file area.
- Frequency Units options.  Choose whether the frequency data in the file is given in Hz (cycles per second) or RPM (cycles per minute). Internally, the program always uses Hz, and results are reported in Hz. Note that the frequency units also affect the function values, since they are specified per unit of frequency.
- Function graph display area.  This area displays a graph of the function. First specify all of the data in the Function File, Values are and Format type areas. Then click the Display Graph button in the Function Graph area of the form to display the graph of the function.  
    
  Run the mouse pointer over the function graph and a dot appears along the line representing the function. The coordinates of the dot are reported in the box just below the graph.

|  |
| --- |
| Access the Power Spectral Density Function Definition form for a Function Form File as follows:   1. Click the Define menu > Functions > Define Power Spectral Density command to display the Define Power Spectral Density Function form. 2. Select Function from File in the Choose Function Type to Add drop-down list. Then do one of the following:     - Click the Add New Function button.    - Select a previously defined function from file definition in the Functions display area and click the Modify/Show Function button. |

<!-- source: Menus/Define/Functions/Power_Spectral_Density/User_Power_Spectral_Density_Function.htm | User Power Spectral Density Function -->

# User Function - Power Spectral Density Function

When defining a user defined power spectral density function, the Power Spectral Density Function Definition form has the following areas:

- Function name edit box.  Specify the name of the function.
- Frequency Units options.  Choose to specify the frequency as Hz (cycles per second) or RPM (cycles per minute). Internally, the program always uses Hz, and results are reported in Hz. Note that the frequency units also affect the function values, since they are specified per unit of frequency.
- Define Function area.  Input pairs of frequency and function values in this area. Type the Frequency (in the chosen units) and function Value corresponding to a single point of the function into the edit boxes at the top of this area. Then click the Add button. Repeat this process until points have been entered. Enter the points in any order; they will be sorted by ascending frequency. A frequency value may not be duplicated. Function values may not be negative.  
    
  To modify an existing pair of values, first highlight the appropriate values in the list box. Note that when you highlight them, they appear in the edit boxes at the top of the area. Modify the values in the edit boxes and then click the Modify button.  
    
  To delete an existing pair of values, first highlight the appropriate values in the list box.  Then click the Delete button.
- Function graph area.  This area displays a graph of the function. It updates automatically as additional points are defined for the function. If your computer has any problem with the automatic update, click the Display Graph button located just below the graph.  
    
  Run the mouse pointer over the function graph and a dot appears along the line representing the function. The coordinates of the dot are reported in the box just below the graph.

|  |
| --- |
| Access the Power Spectral Density Function Definition form as follows:   1. Click the Define menu > Functions > Define Power Spectral Density command to display the Define Power Spectral Density Function form. 2. Select  User Function in the Choose Function Type to Add drop-down list. Then do one of the following:  1. - Click the Add New Function button.    - Select a previously defined user function definition in the Functions display area and click the Modify/Show Function button. |
