<!-- source: Menus/View/Set_3-D_View.htm | Set 3-D View -->

# Set 3-D View

Form:  Set 3D View

A 3-D view shows all three dimensions of the structure, as viewed from an arbitrary user-specified location. By way of contrast, a 2-D view shows only one plane or surface of the structure.

Use the View menu > Set 3D View command to access the Set 3D View form and set the view in the active window to a 3D View. Alternatively, quickly set the active view to the default 3D view by clicking the 3D button ![](../../assets/images/Images/3DVIEW.GIF).

- Fast Views buttons.  Use these buttons to quickly set the view direction angles. The 3D button sets the default 3-D view, similar to a standard isometric view, but with perspective.

The remaining three buttons set the view direction perpendicular to one of the principal planes in the current coordinate system. However, these are 3-D views showing the full depth of the structure normal to the viewing plane, with perspective.

- View Direction Angle options.  Set these three angles to determine the orientation of the view. These angles can be thought of as describing the location of your eye, looking toward the origin:
- - Plan angle: Your location in the X-Y plane, where zero is on the positive X axis, and 90 is on the positive Y axis.
  - Elevation angle: Your location above or below the X-Y plane, where zero is on the X-Y plane, and 90 is on the positive Z axis.
  - Aperture angle: A measure of how strong the perspective effect is, or how far away you are from the origin. Zero indicates that you are infinitely far away, and all receding lines are parallel (no perspective). A value between 30 and 60 is usually adequate.

The effect of the chosen view direction is shown by the block displayed in the upper left corner of the form.

Note:  Rotate a 3D view by depressing the Ctrl key and the middle mouse button as you move the mouse.

Tips:  Use the [Options menu > 3D View Up Direction command](../Options/3D_View_Up_Direction.md) to select the axis to be drawn in the vertical up direction.

## See Also

[Select 2D View](Set_2-D_View.md)

<!-- source: Menus/View/Set_Display_Options.htm | Set Display Options -->

# Set Display Options

Form:  Display Options for Active Window

The View menu > Set Display Options command or ![](../../assets/images/Images/Set%20Display%20Options%20button.jpg) button accesses the Display Options For Active Window form, which can be used to selectively display various features associated with the objects. Use this method to selectively display various object types, object labels, and certain assignments to the objects. In addition, use the form to control how the objects display (show only edges, interior fill, or a 3-D shaded image). An option is also available to shrink objects away from their connection points (joints) to view the connectivity of the model more readily.

Unless the Apply to All Windows check box is checked, the chosen settings affect only the display in the active window.

Note: If the Not in View check box for an object type is checked, that type of object cannot be graphically selected in the affected view(s). Note that point objects can be present in a view, but be visible or invisible. All other types of objects are visible if they are present in the view.

- Select Groups button. When the Selected Groups option is chosen, the Select Groups button is available. Click that button to access the Select Groups form. Highlight [a group](../Assign/Assign_to_Groups.md) in the Select display area and click the OK button. The active window will be updated to display the chosen group(s) after the OK button on the Display Options for Active Window form is clicked.
- Apply to All Windows check box. Check this check box to apply the selected options to all windows, both active and inactive.
- Show Analysis Model (If Available) check box. Check this check box to display the analysis model.  If the analysis model is not currently available, the program will prompt you to create it.  After changes have been made to the model so that the analysis model is no longer available because it does not reflect the current model status, click the Analyze menu > Create Analysis Model command to create the analysis model.

Additional Considerations

1. The Display Options For Active Windows form is intended to set the view preferences in the default display. The options in this form control the objects present, colors used, and a limited number of assignments, such as sections, restraints, and labels.

   - To see the default display, use the Display > Show Undeformed Shape command, which can also be accessed using the F4 key.
2. Most other assignments are not controlled using the Display Options For Active Windows form. These can be viewed using the Display > Show Load Assigns and Display > Show Misc Assigns commands. Afterwards, the F4 key is used to clear this display and return to the default display.
3. When any assignment is made, this type of assignment is automatically shown for convenience and verification, similar to using the Display > Show Load Assigns and Display > Show Misc Assigns commands. Again, the F4 key can used to return to the default display.

## See Also

[New Labels](../Draw/New_Labels.md)

<!-- source: Menus/View/Set_Limits.htm | Set Limits -->

# Set Limits

Form:  Set Limits

Use the View menu > Set Limits command when you do not want the entire structure to appear in the display. This option allows you to selectively display portions of the structure by defining limits on the X, Y and Z axes viewing range.

1. Click the View menu > Set Limits command to access the Set Limits form.
2. In the Set Limits form use one of the following methods to specify the viewing range:

Method 1

1. 1. Choose one of the XY, YZ and XZ planes.
   2. In the viewing screen that appears in the top left corner of the form, use the mouse to draw a box around the area you want to view. Note that the limits of the box you define will be reflected in the Max and Min range for the corresponding Axis Limits edit boxes.
   3. Choose another of the XY, YZ and XZ planes and repeat Step 2.
   4. Choose the final XY, YZ and XZ plane and repeat Step 2.

Method 2

1. 1. Directly enter in the Max and Min Axis Limits for the X, Y and Z axes.
   2. Click the OK button.

Click the Show All button to reset the full view for the corresponding axis.

Check the Ignore Limit Settings check box to quickly remove limit settings without eliminating them. Use this option to quickly switch the display from a limited view to a full view.

Note: The [View menu > Show Selection Only command](Show_Selection_Only.md) can be used to view only selected members. Use the [View menu > Show All command](Show_All.md) to restore all elements in the model.

Example:  Use of this command is demonstrated in [Problem S](../../Example_Problems/Problem_S.md) and [Problem U](../../Example_Problems/Problem_U.md).

# Show All

Use the View menu > Show All command to remove the effects of the [View menu > Show Selection Only command](Show_Selection_Only.md). In other words, this command shows all objects again.

Note:  Right clicking anywhere in an active window will display a drop-down menu of commands, including the Show All command. Clicking that command is the same as using the View menu > Show All command.

Example:  Use of this command is demonstrated in [Problem U](../../Example_Problems/Problem_U.md).

<!-- source: Menus/View/Show_Selection_Only.htm | Show Selection Only -->

# Show Selection Only

If too many objects are  visible in a view, select the objects you want to view and use the View menu > Show Selection Only command to refresh the view so that only the selected items are visible in the window. If you change the view type in the window, say from a plan view to a 3D view, the originally selected items continue to be the only ones visible.

Use the [View menu > Show All command](Show_All.md) to restore all objects to the view.

Note:  Right clicking anywhere in an active window will display a drop-down menu of commands, including the Show Selection Only command. Clicking that command is the same as using the View menu > Show Selection Only command.  Thus, select objects before right clicking and selecting the Show Selection Only command from the resulting drop-down menu.

Example:  Use of this command is demonstrated in [Problem U](../../Example_Problems/Problem_U.md).

<!-- source: Menus/View/View_Invert_View.htm | View Invert View -->

# View - Invert View Selection

The View menu > Invert View Selection command inverts the objects displayed in a view. Any objects previously displayed in a view will no longer be visible, and objects previously not displayed will become visible.  This command is typically used in conjunction with the View menu > Show Selection Only command.  For example, assume that in a large model only a few objects are not to be displayed.  In that case, it may be easier to select the few objects that are not to be displayed and then use the View menu > Show Selection Only command followed by the View menu > Invert View Selection command to refresh the display such that all objects are visible except for those few originally selected.  If the view type in the window is changed, for example from a plan view to a 3D view, the objects displayed remain the same.

Note:  Right clicking anywhere in an active window will display a drop-down menu of commands, including the Invert View Selection command. Clicking that command is the same as using the View menu > Invert View Selection command.


---
<!-- source: Menus/View/Zoom_Feature.htm | Zoom Feature -->

# Zoom Feature

There are five zoom features available in SAP2000. These features allow zooming in or out on a view. Zooming in shows a closer view of the model and zooming out shows a more distant view of the model. All five zoom features are available both on the View menu and on the toolbar. The zoom features and their associated toolbar buttons are as follows:

Rubber Band Zoom, ![](../../assets/images/Images/IMG00039.GIF) : Use the View menu > Rubber Band Zoom command or associated button to zoom in on the model by windowing. To use the feature, click the button or the command and depress and hold down the left mouse button. While keeping the left button depressed, drag the mouse to "rubber band" a window around the portion of the view that is of interest. A dashed line on the screen shows the extent of the rubber band window. When the left mouse button is released, the new "zoomed" view is displayed.

Tip: Use the F2 key to activate the Rubber Band Zoom.

Restore Full View, ![](../../assets/images/Images/ebx_-661494151.gif):  Use the View menu > Restore Full View command or associated button to re-display the entire structure in the window after any of the Zoom features have been used.

Tip: Use the F3 key to restore the full view.

Previous Zoom,  ![](../../assets/images/Images/IMG00041.GIF) : Use the View menu > Previous Zoom command or associated button to switch to the previously zoomed view, and then back to the current zoomed view if so desired.  Only the active window is affected by this command. In addition, use this command to restore a view if the View menu > Pan command is used to adjust a view in the window. In that case, the [View menu > Previous Zoom command](Previous_Zoom.md) returns the view to the view right before the View menu > Pan command was used.

Zoom In One Step,  ![](../../assets/images/Images/ebx_-1509723921.gif) :   Use the View menu > Zoom In One Step command or associated button to zoom in on a currently active window. The step of the zoom can be set using the [Options menu > Dimensions and Tolerances command](../Options/Dimensions_Tolerances.md). The Zoom Step is input as a percent of the actual and cannot be greater than 100%.

Zoom Out One Step,  ![](../../assets/images/Images/ebx_-968520110.gif) : Use the View menu > Zoom Out One Step command or associated button to zoom out on a currently active window. The step of the zoom can be set using the [Options menu > Dimensions and Tolerances command](../Options/Dimensions_Tolerances.md). The Zoom Step is input as a percent of the actual and cannot be greater than 100%.

Note:  The mouse wheel can be used as a short cut to Zoom In and Zoom Out on a view in the active window. Rotate the wheel forward (away from you) to Zoom In and backward (toward you) to Zoom Out. Depress the Shift key and the middle mouse button while moving the mouse as another short cut to Zoom In and Zoom Out.


---
<!-- source: Menus/View/Zoom_Realtime.htm | Zoom Realtime -->

# Zoom Realtime

Use the View menu > Realtime command is available when the display window is set to OpenGL using the Option menu > Graphics Mode > OpenGL command. When this command is enabled, the mouse wheel can be used to zoom in and out in the active view.

<!-- source: Output/Frame_Element_Internal_Forces_Output_Conventions.htm | Frame Element Internal Forces Output Conventions -->

# Frame Element Internal Forces Output Conventions

The frame internal forces are:

- P, the axial force
- V2, the shear force in the 1-2 plane
- V3, the shear force in the 1-3 plane
- T, the axial torque (about the 1-axis)
- M2, the bending moment in the 1-3 plane (about the 2-axis)
- M3, the bending moment in the 1-2 plane (about the 3-axis)

These internal forces and moments are present at every cross-section along the length of the frame.

For each load pattern and load combination the frame internal forces and moments are computed and reported at each frame output station.

For frame output displayed in a tabular form on the computer screen, printed to a printer or printed to a file, the locations of the output stations are identified by the absolute distance to the station measured from the i-end of the frame.

The sign convention for frame internal forces is illustrated in the figure below. This sign convention can be described by defining the concept of positive and negative faces of an object. Consider a section cut through the object in the 2-3 plane. At this section the positive 1 face is the face whose outward normal (arrow that is perpendicular to the section and pointing away from the section) is in the positive local 1 direction. At this same section the negative 1 face is one whose outward normal is in the negative local 1 direction. The positive 2 and 3 faces are those faces with outward normals in the positive local 2 and 3 directions, respectively, from the neutral axis. Note the following about the frame internal forces:

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_1134753510.JPG)

- Positive internal forces (P, V2 and V3) and positive axial torque (T) acting on a positive 1 face are oriented in the positive direction of the corresponding object local coordinate axis. For example, when V2 acting on a positive 1 face is positive, it is oriented in the direction of the positive local 2-axis.

- Positive internal forces (P, V2 and V3) and positive axial torque (T) acting on a negative 1 face are oriented in the negative direction of the corresponding object local coordinate axis. For example, when V2 acting on a negative 1 face is positive, it is oriented in the direction of the negative local 2-axis.

- Positive M2 bending moments cause compression on the positive 3 face and tension on the negative 3 face.

- Positive M3 bending moments cause compression on the positive 2 face and tension on the negative 2 face.

- When end offsets along the length of the frame are present, the internal forces and moments are output at the faces of the supports rather than the ends of the object. No output is produced within the end offset length.

- The right-hand rule applies in the figure for determining the sense of the moments shown by the double arrows.

<!-- source: Output/Joint_Element_Output_Conventions.htm | Joint Element Output Conventions -->

# Joint Element Output Conventions

- Spring Force Output Conventions. Spring forces are reported as forces acting on the elements connected to the support. They are reported with respect to the joint local coordinate system. Positive spring forces act in the same direction as the positive local axes. The sense of positive moments can be determined using the right-hand rule.
- Support Reaction Output Conventions. Support reactions are reported as forces acting on the elements connected to the support. The reaction forces are reported with respect to the joint local coordinate system. Positive support reaction forces act in the same direction as the positive local axes. The sense of positive moments can be determined using the right-hand rule.

Note: By default, joint local axes 1, 2 and 3 align with the global coordinate system X, Y and Z axes, as long as local axis rotations have not been assigned to the joint.

As an example, consider a building column that is supporting gravity load. This gravity load acts in a downward direction. Thus the force imposed on the bottom of the column acts in an upward direction. This is the reaction force reported by SAP2000. Since the upward force is in the same direction as the positive joint local 3 axis, the reaction is reported as a positive value acting in the 3 direction.

The figure below illustrates positive support reaction forces.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_676387730.JPG)

<!-- source: Output/Panel_Zone_Output_Conventions.htm | Panel Zone Output Conventions -->

# Panel Zone Output Conventions

Internally in the analysis model, SAP2000 creates two joints at locations where [panel zones are assigned to point objects](../Menus/Assign/Joint/Joint_Panel_Zones.md). If the panel zone is between columns and other objects, one of the joints is connected to the columns and one is connected to the other object. Brace-to-other-object panel zones are similar.

SAP2000 reports panel zone displacements (using the [Display menu > Show Miscellaneous Assigns > Joints command](../Menus/Display/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns/Show_Miscellaneous_Assigns_Joints.md) and the Panel Zone option), panel zone internal deformations and panel zone internal forces (using the [Display menu > Show Tables command](../Database_Tables/Choose_Tables_For_Form.md) and the Analysis Results, Element Output, Panel Output option). Do not confuse panel zone displacements and internal deformations. They are different.

- Panel Zone Displacements

SAP2000 reports displacements for a point object with a panel zone assignment as follows:

1. - Beam-to-Other-Object Connectivity: Displacements are reported for the joint connected to the column.
   - Brace-to-Other-Object Connectivity: Displacements are reported for the joint connected to the column.

Panel zone displacements are reported in the global coordinate system. Positive translational displacements are in the same direction as the positive global axes. The sense of positive rotations can be determined using the right-hand rule.

- Panel Zone Internal Deformations

Panel zone internal deformations are reported in the [panel zone local coordinate system.](../Menus/Assign/Joint/Joint_Panel_Zones.md#Local_Axis) The following conventions are used by SAP2000:

1. - Beam-to-Other-Object Connectivity: The i-end of the panel zone is the joint that is connected to the columns. The j-end of the panel zone is the joint that is connected to the other object.
   - Brace-to-Other-Object Connectivity: The i-end of the panel zone is the joint that is connected to the other object. The j-end of the panel zone is the joint that is connected to the brace.

- Panel Zone Internal Forces

The panel zone internal forces indicate how much unbalanced load is transferred through the panel zone. For example, in a panel zone with beam-to-other-object connectivity the internal forces indicate how much unbalanced moment is transferred from the beams to the other objects.

Panel zone internal forces are calculated as described for [link element internal forces](Link_Element_Internal_Force_Output_Convention.md). Since panel zone elements are zero length, elements M2 = M2b and M3 = M3b. The panel zone internal forces are reported in the panel zone local coordinate system.

<!-- source: Output/Section_Cut_Output_Conventions.htm | Section Cut Output Conventions -->

# Section Cut Output Conventions

Section cut forces are reported at a single point in the local coordinate system defined for the section cut. Six different force components are reported at that single point. They are:

- F1: A force in the section cut local 1-axis direction.
- F2: A force in the section cut local 2-axis direction.
- F3: A force in the section cut local 3-axis direction.
- M1: A moment about the section cut local 1-axis.
- M2: A moment about the section cut local 2-axis.
- M3: A moment about the section cut local 3-axis.

Section cut forces are reported as forces acting on the objects that make up the group that defines the section cut. An example of this is described below. Positive section forces act in the same direction as the positive section cut local axes. The sense of positive moments can be determined using the right-hand rule.

Consider the example shown in the figure below. The global coordinate system axes and the section cut local coordinate system axes are shown in Figure a. This illustrates that the local coordinate system axes may be different from the global system.

![](../assets/images/Images/EBX_1931321257.gif)

Figure b shows a floor system that consists of 9 area objects labeled F1 through F9 and 16 associated point objects labeled 1 through 16. Suppose that we want to determine the section cut forces through the floor system at the location identified by the heavy line in Figure c. This section cut passes through the point objects labeled 3, 7, 11 and 15.

Two groups can be defined for use in the section cut definition. Figure d shows the first possible group, which includes area objects F2, F5 and F8 and point objects 3, 7, 11 and 15. Figure e shows free body diagrams that define the positive direction of section cut forces when the section cut is defined using the group definition shown in Figure d. Note that the positive section cut forces acting on the left free body diagram are in the same direction as the positive section cut local axes shown in Figure a. The left free body diagram is the one that includes the objects that were used to define the group that defined the section cut.

Figure f shows the second possible group that could define the section cut. This group includes area objects F3, F6 and F9 and point objects 3, 7, 11 and 15. Figure g shows free body diagrams that define the positive direction of section cut forces when the section cut is defined using the group definition shown in f. Note that the positive section cut forces acting on the right free body diagram are in the same direction as the positive section cut local axes shown in Figure a. The right free body diagram is the one that includes the objects that were used to define the group that defined the section cut.

<!-- source: Output/Shell_Element_Internal_Forces_Stresses_Output_Convention.htm | Shell Element Internal Forces Stresses Output Convention -->

# Shell Element Internal Forces/Stresses Output Convention

The six faces of a shell element are defined as the
positive 1 face, negative 1 face, positive 2 face, negative 2 face, positive
3 face and negative 3 face as shown in the figure below. In this definition
the numbers 1, 2 and 3 correspond to the [local
axes](../Menus/Assign/Area/Area_Local_Axes.md) of the shell element. The positive 1 face of the element is the
face that is perpendicular to the 1-axis of the element whose outward
normal (pointing away from the element) is in the positive 1-axis direction.
The negative 1 face of the element is a face that is perpendicular to
the 1-axis of the element whose outward normal (pointing away from the
element) is in the negative 1-axis direction. The other faces have similar
definitions.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_-556935993.gif)

Note that the positive 3 face is sometimes called
the top of the shell element in SAP2000, particularly in the output, and
the negative 3 face is called the bottom of the shell element.

[Shell
Element Internal Forces](javascript:TextPopup(this))

The shell element internal forces, like stresses,
act throughout the element. They are present at every point on the
midsurface of the shell element. SAP reports values for the shell
internal forces at the element nodes. It is important to note that
the internal forces are reported as forces and moments per unit of
in-plane length.

The basic shell element forces and moments are
identified as F11, F22, F12, M11, M22, M12, V13 and V23. You might
expect that there would also be an F21 and M21, but F21 is always
equal to F12 and M21 is always equal to M12, so it is not actually
necessary to report F21 and M21.

The figure below shows internal F11 forces acting
on the midsurface of a shell element. In the figure, the force distribution
labeled (a) represents an actual F11 force distribution. The force
distribution labeled (b) shows how SAP2000 calculates only the internal
forces at the corner points of the shell element. Note that we could
calculate these stresses at any location on the shell element. We
simply choose to calculate them only at the corner points because
that is a convenient location and it keeps the amount of output to
a reasonable volume.

![](../assets/images/Images/Shell%20Internal%20Forces%202.bmp)

The force distribution labeled (c) in the figure
above shows how SAP2000 assumes that the F11 forces vary linearly
along the length of the shell element between the calculated F11 force
values at the element nodes for graphical plotting purposes only.

The figure below illustrates the positive directions
for shell element internal forces F11, F22, F12, V13 and V23. Note that these shell element internal
forces are forces per unit length acting on the midsurface of the
shell element. SAP2000 reports only the value of these forces at the
shell element corner points.

![](../assets/images/Images/Shell%20Internal%20Forces%203.bmp)

The figure below illustrates the positive direction
for shell element principal forces, Fmax and Fmin. It also illustrates
the positive direction for the shell element maximum transverse shear
force, Vmax.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_-1108120400.gif)

For values of V13 and V23 at any angle, the maximum
transverse shear stress, V-Max, can be calculated as:

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_-1324632104.gif)

The figure below illustrates the positive directions
for shell element internal moments M11, M22 and M12. Note that these
shell element internal moments are moments per unit length acting
on the midsurface of the shell element. SAP2000 reports only the value
of these moments per unit length at the shell element corner points.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_824428348.gif)

Use the right-hand rule to determine the sense
of the moments shown in the figure above.

The figure below illustrates the positive direction
for shell element principal moments, Mmax and Mmin.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_1797286568.gif)

See Also:

[Sign
Convention](../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Sign_Convention.md)

[Shell
Element Internal Stresses](javascript:TextPopup(this))

The basic shell element stresses are identified
as S11, S22, S12, S13, and S23. An S21 might also be expected, but
S21 is always equal to S12, so it is not actually necessary to report
S21. Sij stresses (where i can be equal
to 1 or 2 and j can be equal to 1, 2 or 3) are stresses that occur
on face i of an element in direction j. Direction j refers to the
local axis direction of the shell element. Thus S11 stresses occur
on face 1 of the element (perpendicular to the local 1 axis) and are
acting in the direction parallel to the local 1 axis (that is, the
stresses act normal to face 1). As another example, S12 stresses occur
on face 1 of the element (perpendicular to the local 1 axis) and are
acting in the direction parallel to the local 2 axis (that is, the
stresses act parallel to face 1, like shearing stresses). The figure
below shows examples of each of these basic types of shell stresses.
SAP2000 reports internal stresses for shell elements at the four corner
points of the appropriate face of the element. For example, refer
to Figure a below. On the positive 1 face internal stresses are reported
by SAP2000 at points A, B, C and D.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_1142683448.gif)

Shell internal stresses are reported for both
the top and the bottom of the shell element. The top and bottom of
the element are defined relative to the local 3-axis of the element.
The positive 3-axis side of the element is considered to be the top
of the element. Thus in Figure a above, internal stresses at the top
of the element include stresses at the joints labeled A and C and
internal stresses at the bottom of the element include stresses at
the joints labeled B and D. The Figure below clearly illustrates the
points where SAP2000 reports the shell element internal stress values.

![](../assets/images/Images/Shell%20Internal%20Stresses.bmp)

The transverse shear stresses calculated by SAP2000
(S13 and S23) are average values. The actual transverse shear stress
distribution is approximately parabolic; it is zero at the top and
bottom surfaces and has its maximum or minimum value at the midsurface
of the element. SAP2000 reports the average transverse shear value.
An approximation to the maximum (or minimum) transverse shear stress
would be 1.5 times the average shear stress.

The figure below illustrates the positive directions
for shell element internal stresses S11, S22, S12, S13 and S23. Also
shown are the positive directions for the principal stresses, S-Max and S-Min, and the
positive directions for the maximum transverse shear stresses, S-Max-V.

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_-434685189.gif)

For values of S13 and S23 at any angle, the maximum
transverse shear stress, S-MaxV, can
be calculated from:

![](../assets/images/Images/ebx_-1671004901.gif)

See Also:

[Sign
Convention](../Keyboard_Commands_and_Special_Features/Sign_Convention.md)
